Let’s talk about something that’s at the heart of how we all handle money—self-awareness.
Money is so much more than numbers in a bank account. It’s personal. It’s tangled up with our beliefs, our habits, and emotions—many of which we barely notice.
Think about it: how often do you catch yourself just going through the motions? Maybe you’re spending or saving the way you always have, and you’re not even sure why. A lot of us pick up patterns in childhood or simply copy the people around us, never really stopping to ask, “Does this work for me?”
Real change? It starts when you’re willing to look inward and get curious about what’s driving your choices.
Here’s a story that brings this to life. There was a woman who always felt anxious whenever she spent money—even if she had plenty in the bank. She started digging into where that anxiety came from, and realized it went all the way back to her parents. They struggled with money, worried about every single purchase, and she’d soaked up those fears without even realizing it. Once she understood the roots of her anxiety, she could make choices with her eyes wide open. She found a way to balance being cautious with actually enjoying her life.
Most of us don’t realize just how much these invisible scripts shape our money habits. Maybe you spend money to feel loved, or you save every penny to feel safe. Or maybe, you avoid thinking about money altogether, hoping those tricky problems just disappear.
But the more you get to know what’s really motivating you, the easier it becomes to make decisions that truly serve you—not just the old habits or stories you’ve been carrying around.
Self-awareness isn’t about beating yourself up or blaming anyone. It’s about approaching your own habits with a sense of curiosity. Ask yourself, “Why do I do what I do? Is this actually helping me, or holding me back?”
Sure, this process can feel a little uncomfortable. Looking at your beliefs and patterns honestly isn’t always easy. But it’s also incredibly freeing. When you understand yourself better, you get back in the driver’s seat. Suddenly, you have more control over your financial life.
Over time, self-awareness has a way of transforming your relationship with money. You’ll find yourself reacting less—making choices that are intentional and that actually line up with your values. The journey isn’t always smooth, but it’s the foundation for real, lasting change.
